display_title: Official Review of Paper4625 by Reviewer 1ggR

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a variant of Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) in the context of federated learning by considering different weights of each device loss. It provides convergence guarantees for the solver, and empirically demonstrates the effectiveness of the objective on standard benchmarks.
content.main_review:
* Title is too general: any work in the area of fair FL can be called fairness-aware federated learning

* The submission describes the flexible tradeoff between accuracy and fairness as one of the major contributions of HCVaR throughout (e.g., after Definition 1, in the experiments, etc), which is misleading. The flexible tradeoff is brought about by CVaR, and HCVaR inherits such properties because it is a direct extension of CVaR. In other words, this benefit is not due to the fact that HCVaR allows for different alpha_i's, which is the only difference between CVaR and HCVaR. For instance, the example given under Eq (1) where FAFL reduces to previous objectives is a property of distributionally robust optimization (or its dual, classic CVaR), not a new property of HCVaR. 

* HCVaR changes alpha in CVaR to alpha_i's. I understand it is scaling the probability of each device's loss by some constant, but it is hard to reason about the effective behavior of HCVaR_{1-alpha}. Compared with CVaR, which only has alpha as an interpretable hyperparameter, alpha_i's introduce one hyperparameter per device.

* The motivation/benefits of using the smooth approximation are not clear. Standard solvers for CVaR (e.g., those mentioned in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.05893.pdf) are readily applicable to solve HCVaR. For general convex functions, this approximation does not seem to improve convergence rates (1/\eps^2) theoretically. Empirical benefits of solving this variant (if there are any) are also missing. In addition, the convergence error (related to mu) might be large---there is a 1/mu in L and mu in the last term in Theorem 1. 

* By assuming convexity of f_i's and therefore convexity of HCVaR with respect to (w, eta), there are no challenges in the convergence analysis (i.e., can readily use previous federated optimization analysis). In addition, the algorithms and analysis do not support stochastic cases, which is important for FL.

* The dual representation, the approximation, and the bounds on the approximation (lemma 2) are standard and well-studied in previous literature. Using alpha_i's everywhere does not add additional challenges, and the empirical benefits are not very convincing (see below).

* Experiments should also compare with the objective of directly reweighting losses and CVaR, which are two components of HCVaR.

Others:

* Mischaracterization of several works:

-- 'q-FFL is not a fairness-aware objective' is not justified. The reference Yang et al. (2020) mentioned in the submission studies how system heterogeneity (defined and simulated in a slightly more fine-grained way) impacts various FL algorithms, and I do not think its takeaway is 'q-FFL is less effective in ensuring better fairness under heterogeneity'.

-- For TERM, sampling from a Gumbel-Softmax distribution is not expensive, and they propose efficient stochastic solvers for the objective.

-- 'Li et al. (2021b) do not have fairness guarantees for the fairness benefits except on a linear problem' is correct, but the submission does not have any fairness guarantees on any problem instances.
content.summary_of_the_review: It looks like the proposed formulation does not offer new methodology, techniques, or empirical insights to the studied problem. My main concerns are listed in the comments.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper4625 by Reviewer 1ggR

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1ggR
content.comment:
Thank you for the valuable input. Below, we provide answers to the reviewer’s questions.

> The benefits of HCVaR.

In federated learning setting, because of client heterogeneity, we may wish to treat losses arising from different clients differently. HCVaR allows us to achieve this. For example, we can choose small $\alpha_i$ for an underrepresent client in the population such that that client can be upweighted in optimization to achieve better performance and thus improve fairness. Moreover, we clarify that our FAFL allows each client to choose different $\alpha_i$ for gaining more flexibility and taking into account heterogeneity. In practice, especially when the number of clients is large, we can choose the same $\alpha$ for each client and thus only need to tune one hyperparameter, which is feasible and affordable. Allowing different $\alpha_i$ for each client would be very helpful if we have some prior knowledge about which client’s data is the hardest one to distinguish from others. For example, in Fashion-MNIST, it is known that the shirt class is hardest one. Thus we can choose small $\alpha_i$ for that client to highlight its importance in achieving fairness as in Table 3. 

> The motivation of using smooth approximation.

We clarify that our paper focuses more on theory, and the introduction of smoothing enables us to develop a theoretically proven convergent algorithm. Despite that existing solver like the one mentioned by the reviewer can solve CVaR with convergence guarantees in traditional (centralized) machine learning, it is not applicable to federated learning setting considered in our paper as it requires frequent communication. For example, in the solver mentioned by the reviewer, the sampled clients (min-batch) need to share data with each other to compute the gradient of the surrogate loss.  In fact, smoothness is a standard assumption to prove convergence in federated learning. Thus, we consider solving a smooth approximation which is proven to find a minimizer of the original objective as shown in Theorem 1&2. 

Empirically, on Sent140 dataset, the average, worst 10$%$, Best $10%$ and variance of the test accuracy for solving the original CVaR directly using subgradient-based methods are 69.9%, 26.7%, 100.0% and 505 respectively, which is worse than our proposed algorithm but still be better than other baselines. 

Finally, the convergence rate would not be too large as the reviewer might be concerned. If we choose $\mu={\epsilon}/{2\tau_\alpha}$, then after $T_N=\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon^2)$ rounds of communication between clients and server, our algorithm can  achieve a $\epsilon$-approximate solution.

> The convergence analysis.

Despite that Khaled et al. (2019) has derived the convergence bound for convex loss in federated optimization, their result is limited to full participation case. However, we further consider the case of partial participation where only a subset of clients performs local updates. The partial participation case is more practical especially when the number of clients is large. We derive a convergence rate for that in Theorem 2 whereas partial participation is not considered in Khaled et al. (2019). We should mention that the analysis for partial participation is much more complicated as the randomly selected subset of clients varies each round. To overcome this difficulty, we introduce a virtual sequence and rewrite the update rule of algorithm 1.

> The dual representation, the approximation, and the bounds on the approximation are standard. And the experiments should compare with CVaR.

Despite that CVaR as a fairness risk measure have been studied in prior work, it has never been explored in federated learning. We are the first to consider fairness in terms of CVaR in federated learning. We also generalize CVaR and define a new notion HCVaR which takes into account client heterogeneity and is more related to federated learning setting. To the best of our knowledge, this notion has not been considered in prior work. Finally, although some algorithms have been proposed to solve CVaR in traditional (centralized) machine learning, they are not applicable to federated learning setting considered in our paper as it requires frequent communication. And we are the first to propose a theoretically principled algorithm which can be efficiently implemented to solve this problem in FL and provide generalization guarantees. In the experiments, we have reported the performance of CVaR, i.e, FAFL with the same $\alpha_i$s.

content.title: continued
content.comment:
> q-FFL is not a fairness-aware objective.

An objective $f(\omega)$ is fairness-aware if it can be written as $f(\omega)=L(\omega)+D(\omega)$ where $L(\omega)$ is the standard expected risk and $D(\omega)$ is a fairness measure. In this sense, our FAFL is fairness-aware while $q$-FFL is not. (see last line of P4). And, the sentence “q-FFL is less effective in ensuring better fairness under heterogeneity” is mentioned by Yang et al. (2020) in the last line (R) of P6.


> Comparison to TERM.

Our algorithm is a simple gradient descent and can be efficiently implemented in federated setting with strong theoretical guarantees, whereas TERM requires dynamically sampling from a Gumbel-Softmax distribution and dynamically reweighting the samples and clients (involving computing normalization weights) in local updates and averaging step at each communication round.

> Fairness guarantees. 

Our FAFL is a fairness risk measure with fairness-aware objective, i.e., $f_\alpha(\omega)=E[f^i(\omega)]+D_\alpha(f^i(\omega))$ where $D_\alpha(f^i(\omega))=CVaR_{1-\alpha}(f^i(\omega)- E[f^i(\omega)])$ is a regular and coherent  deviation (fairness) measure. Using KKT conditions, we may equivalently rewrite our FAFL problem as a constrained optimization problem, i.e., $\min E[f^i(\omega)]$ such that $D_\alpha(f^i(\omega))\leq \epsilon$ for some $\epsilon$. Therefore, minimizing our objective is equivalent to find $\omega$ minimizing the expected loss subject to the fairness measure being smaller than $\epsilon$.

content.title: followups
content.comment:
Thanks for the response. I think my major concerns still remain, and I listed some of them below.

(1) Regarding the role of alpha_i's, it is not clear to me how we should reason about the benefits of using CVaR and allowing for different alpha_i's. In the Fashion-MNIST example, probably just solving for CVaR would suffice to upweight the minority class (rare events). Providing specific applications where the additional benefits of having varying alpha_i's is significant compared with only applying CVaR could help clarify this point. I still think tuning alpha_i's is hard---[if tuning it locally] devices have no information of whether their local datasets should be up-weighted or down-weighted; and [if tuning it centrally] the server has to set one hyperparameter per device.

(2) Regarding the convergence analysis, I agree this work has some improvements over Khaled et al. (2019). In my original review, I was referring to the analyses in the vast existing FL optimization literature where allowing for partial participation and local updating and the use of virtual sequences are standard (A Field Guide to Federated Optimization, Wang et al.). 

(3) The claim 'Despite that CVaR as a fairness risk measure have been studied in prior work, it has never been explored in federated learning.' is not correct, as Laguel et al. (2020) is also solving for CVaR. 

Therefore, I maintain my original score.

display_title: Official Review of Paper4625 by Reviewer smE9

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new federated learning objective for promoting fairness. The new objective introduces client level hyperparameters $\alpha_i$, which in turn can recover federated averaging by setting $\alpha_i = 1$ and agnostic federated learning (AFL) by setting $\alpha_i = \frac{1}{p_i}$ where $p_i$ is the client-level weight. The paper draws connections between the proposed objective and a generalized form of Conditional-Value-at-Risk (CVaR). Then, the paper proposes a federated solver for the new objective, proves its convergence at full client participation as well as partial client participation, and proves generalization bounds for the objective. The paper ends with experiments in federated benchmarks where it demonstrates the superior performance of the proposed algorithm compared to FedAvg, AFL, and q-FFL (Li et al., 2020).
content.main_review:
This paper proposes a new federated learning objective for promoting fairness. The new objective introduces client level hyperparameters $\alpha_i$, which in turn can recover federated averaging by setting $\alpha_i = 1$ and agnostic federated learning (AFL) by setting $\alpha_i = \frac{1}{p_i}$ where $p_i$ is the client-level weight. The paper draws connections between the proposed objective and a generalized form of Conditional-Value-at-Risk (CVaR). 


- It is unclear to me what the operational meaning of the vector $\alpha$ is, beyond being a set of hyperparameters that reweight CVaR. In particular, what is the operational meaning of the new CVaR variant, the so-called heterogeneous CVaR, beyond it being the dual of the proposed objective?
- There are intimate connections between distributionally robust optimization, and that of CVaR (one being the dual of the other). These connections are known, and pointers to existing literature on that front are missing. For example, (Curi et al., 2020 -- Adaptive Sampling for Stochastic Risk-Averse Learning, NeurIPS 2020) and the references therein.

- One of the most closely related pieces of prior work to this paper is (Laguel et al. 2020), which is on solving superquantile optimization in federated learning. This paper is only referred to very casually on page 6, and is missing from the rest of the paper. Tilted empirical risk minimization (Li et al., 2021) also establishes connections with super-quantile optimization which is not discussed here.



Then, the paper proposes a federated solver for the new objective, proves its convergence at full client participation as well as partial client participation, and proves generalization bounds for the objective. However, unfortunately, the relationship between this solver and existing work has not been properly established.
- As the paper explains, the proposed solver is different from the min-max solver of AFL. The paper claims that this solver is more efficient than that of AFL, however, this claim is neither theoretically nor empirically substantiated.
- There are existing solvers for CVaR, again see (Curi et al., 2020 -- Adaptive Sampling for Stochastic Risk-Averse Learning, NeurIPS 2020) and the references therein. It is not clear to me that the proposed solver in this paper is better in any way (theoretically or empirically).
- The convergence results are only derived for convex losses. This limitation needs to be clearly discussed. What is the difficulty of extending the results beyond convex losses?
- Can you please add a discussion on comparison between the convergence results with those of FedAvg and AFL? 
- It is not clear to me that the bound in Theorem 3 is better than the bound by (Mohri et al., 2019) in any way, especially given the multiplicative factor $\tau_\alpha$ in (6). Can you please compare Theorem 3 with that of AFL in a concrete setting?
- Please make the discussion at the end of Section 5.1.1 explicit, as one needs to have a recipe for choosing the hyperparameter $\mu$, which is not provided here.

The paper ends with experiments in federated benchmarks where it demonstrates the superior performance of the proposed algorithm compared to FedAvg, AFL, and q-FFL (Li et al., 2020).
- First, the baselines (Li et al., 2021) and (Laguel et al. 2020) are missing.
- *Most crucially about this paper*, given that the proposed algorithm has $n$ hyperparameters, where $n$ is the total number of devices, it is crucial to devise a hyperparameter tuning strategy which is completely missing from this paper. This is in contrast to AFL (with no hyperparameters) and q-FFL (with 1 hyperparameter).
- The performance of the proposed strategy vastly varies with hyperparameters as can be seen from Table 3, which makes it even more crucial to devise a systematic strategy for tuning the vector $\alpha$.
- How did you choose the hyperparameter $q$ in q-FFL?
- The paper mentions the following statement: “Our framework is flexible in that it allows each client to select different $\alpha_i$  to trade-off between average accuracy and fairness.” This is misleading as if a client optimizes their $\alpha_i$ for their own best average accuracy, that will probably cost other clients their performance which is the opposite of fairness. Please either justify or remove this claim.

Other comments
- Please clarify what this means on page 2: “ Instead of optimizing the model for a specific (uniform) distribution.
- New notation is introduced in different places, e.g., end of page 3 or beginning of Sec 5.1. Please move all to the notation subsection.
-  The objective at the end of page (4) is distributionally robust optimization (DRO). Please make the connection explicit.
- Please change deviance (pg.5 first line) to deviation.
- Please consider changing the name of the algo, rFedFair, to something that is more closely related to the objective. Too many names are floating around.

====== update ====

Unfortunately, the authors have not revised the paper. While the authors provide partial answers to some of my questions (many remain unaddressed), as I mentioned before, there are major revisions needed before this paper could be published. First and foremost, the paper needs more comprehensive comparison with existing CVaR solvers; and also it should compare with  (Li et al., 2021) and (Laguel et al. 2020). In its current form, it is unclear what the advantage of the proposed solver is compared to existing art. Hence, I remain my reject vote.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, this paper provides a new objective that can be viewed as an extension of FedAvg and AFL (and recovers them both at extremes). The paper develops an algorithmic framework for solving the objective, provides guarantees about the solver, and shows its good performance in federated benchmarks. However, the paper suffers from major shortcomings. Most crucially, the proposed framework comes with $n$ (number of clients) hyperparameters and it is not clear how one should choose these hyperparameters in practice. Some pointers to existing literature about the objective and the solver are missing, and it is unclear whether the proposed solver has advantages over existing solvers. Some of the most closely related literature are missing from comparisons, namely (Laguel et al. 2020) and (Li et al., 2021), which have a far smaller number of hyperparameters. There are major revisions needed to address some of these explicit issues I have raised, hence my reject score.

content.title: Response to Reviewer smE9
content.comment:
We appreciate the insightful comments by the reviewer. Below, we provide responses to the concerns.

> Comparison to Laguel et al. (2020).

First, our algorithm is completely different from theirs in the sense that our algorithm is more like local gradient descent whereas their algorithm is an alternating minimization. Second, although that Laguel et al. (2020) provides convergence analysis for the alternating minimization algorithm (i.e., Algorithm 1), it is not practical and cannot be implemented in the case of federated learning as the authors mentioned. The authors then give a heuristic algorithm (i.e., Algorithm 2) for use in experiments. But there is no theoretical guarantees. In contrast, our algorithm not only enjoys theoretical guarantees including convergence and generalization bounds but also can be efficiently implemented in a federated learning setting. 

> Comparison to Li et al., (2021).

Thanks. We first clarify that the TERM framework proposed by Li et al., (2021) aims to solve traditional (centralized) machine learning problem rather than federated learning, and their algorithm is not very suitable for federated learning problem in practice especially when the number of clients is large as it requires dynamically sampling from a Gumbel-Softmax distribution (or the participation of all clients), which is computationally prohibitive, and dynamically reweighting the samples and clients (involving computing normalization weights) in local updates and averaging step at each communication round respectively is also very expensive. Thus, Li et al., (2021) considers applying their method only to a simple federated learning problem (vehicle dataset with 23 clients) in Appendix. In contrast, we focus on federated learning problem, and our algorithm is a simple gradient descent and can be efficiently implemented in federated setting with strong theoretical guarantees. Empirically, in vehicle dataset, the average, worst 10, Best 10 and standard deviation of our accuracy are 0.876, 0.734, 0.943 and 0.06 respectively, which is better than the accuracy distribution 0.853, 0.707, 0.926, 0.06 of their method. Second, our framework is a worst-case weighted aggregated loss over an uncertainty set, whereas the TERM objective proposed in Li et al., (2021) is a smooth approximation to the maximum function. Besides, we provide theoretical analysis for our framework including convergence guarantees and generalization bound whereas such theoretical results are not given in theirs. 

> Compare the generalization bound (i.e., Theorem 3) with that of AFL?

We clarify that the other terms in our risk bound except the first one is strictly better than that of AFL. Specifically, AFL uses covering-number based analysis to derive a risk bound where they first consider a $\iota$-cover of the simplex and then applies a union bound over this covering. As a result, their bound has an additional non-vanishing term $B\iota$ and also an extra factor $\sqrt{n\log 1/\iota}$ to the high probability (last) term. To overcome this limitation, we propose to exploit the relationship between $Q_\alpha$-weighted loss and averaged client losses to provide a bound without invoking a covering, thus avoiding incurring this non-vanishing term and extra factor, but at the expense of constant-factor to the first term. Despite of that, we highlight that our proof technique is different.

> How to tune the hyperparameters $\alpha_i$?

We first clarify that our FAFL allows each client to choose different $\alpha_i$ for gaining more flexibility and taking into account heterogeneity. In practice, especially when the number of clients is large, we can choose the same $\alpha$ for each client and thus only need to tune one hyperparameter, which is feasible and affordable. For example, in Vehicle and Sent140, we choose the same $\alpha$ for all (or most) clients and then only tune this common $\alpha$ or just generate random $\alpha_i$. And our algorithm still achieves good performance as shown in Table 4. When the number of clients is small, we can search the best $\alpha_i$s for each client on a grid and then report the best performance. Allowing different $\alpha_i$ for each client would be very helpful if we have some prior knowledge about which client’s data is the hardest one to distinguish from others. For example, in Fashion-MNIST, it is known that the shirt class is hardest one. Thus we can choose small $\alpha_i$ for that client to highlight its importance in achieving fairness as in Table 3. 

> What is the operational meaning of HCVaR? 

In federated learning setting, because of client heterogeneity, we may wish to treat losses arising from different clients differently. HCVaR allows us to achieve this. For example, we can choose small $\alpha_i$ for an underrepresent client in the population such that that client can be upweighted in optimization to achieve better performance and thus improve fairness.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer smE9

content.title: Continued
content.comment:
> Why our solver is more efficient than min-max solver of AFL?

The min-max solver of AFL is more like a conventional distributed learning setting where the local models are uploaded to the server at each iteration. Therefore, it requires frequent communication, which is not desirable in federated learning setting due to unreliable and relatively slow network connection. In contrast, our algorithm significantly reduces the number of communications as the local model of clients are aggregated periodically, i.e., one communication every $\kappa$ iterations.

> How our solver compare to existing CVaR solver (e.g., Curi et al., (2020))?

We first clarify that our algorithm focuses on federated learning problem whereas most existing CVaR solvers including that of Curi et al., (2020) considers traditional (centralized) machine learning setting. Therefore, these existing solvers (usually requiring frequent communication) cannot be directly applied to our problem. Besides, the solver of Curi et al., (2020) need to update an adaptive sampler (i.e, K-DPP) using a bandit algorithm for choosing data points (or clients), which is more expensive than our sampling with replacement strategy (the sampling probabilities are fixed), especially when the number of client is large.

> How did you choose the hyperparameter $q$ in q-FFL?

We tune a best q for q-FFL following the same procedure as (Li et al., 2020a) and report its best performance.

> The statement “Our framework is flexible … trade-off between average accuracy and fairness.” is misleading. And what is the meaning of “Instead of optimizing the model for a specific (uniform) distribution.”?

The statement “Our framework is flexible …” means: if we let $\alpha_i\rightarrow p_i$, FAFL reduce to good-intend fairness; as $\alpha_i\rightarrow 1$, FAFL becomes average accuracy. Therefore we can trade-off between average accuracy and fairness by choosing $a_i\in [p_i,1]$. The claim “ Instead of optimizing the model for a specific (uniform) distribution” means that the traditional federated learning objective is to minimize a weighted loss with respect to a uniform distribution whereas our objective is to minimize a worst-case weighted loss over an uncertainty set.

display_title: Official Review of Paper4625 by Reviewer KuJa

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, a fair federated learning algorithm is introduced to address the data heterogeneous issue across the clients. A modified conditional value at risk called heterogeneous conditional value at risk is firstly introduced to define the fairness across the heterogeneous clients. Then an optimization framework called FAFL is proposed to minimize clients' loss while taking into account fairness. Some theoretical results and convergence analysis of the proposed method have been established.
content.main_review:
I have the following major concerns to accept this paper.

1. The motivation for using HCVaR is not clear to me. Since the data distribution is heterogeneous, we could expect the models are different across the clients to a unified fair performance on all the clients. However, in the proposed method, a unified model is trained with empirical weights to achieve the different levels of fairness across the clients.  
2. In addition, how to set proper $\alpha_i$ to guarantee the desired fairness across the clients? What's the reason to have different $\alpha_i$? Why will the clients accept these different settings? 
3. The ablation studies on the parameter $\alpha_i$ are not completed systematically. It is hard to observe the trade-off between fairness and accuracy in the current experiments.
4. The paper is not well-written. For example, in the beginning, FAFL is defined as a framework, and HCVaR is defined as a risk value but the conclusion claims that these two terms are equivalent.
content.summary_of_the_review:
1. The motivation of this work should be further clarified.
2. The experiments need to be done more systematically. 
3. The writing should be improved.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper4625 by Reviewer KuJa

content.title: Response to Reviewer KuJa
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and would like to answer the reviewer’s questions as follows.

> The motivation for using HCVaR is not clear to me.

Thanks. We clarify our motivation as follows. First, the goal of a typical federated learning is to learn a unified model collaboratively while keeping data localized.  However, because of data heterogeneity, the objective function (i.e., the mixture weight) that FL seeks to optimize is unknown. Mohri et al. (2019) argue that the uniform weighting is not the natural target objective and that minimizing with respect to that is risky. Besides, the uniformly weighted loss puts less weight on clients with small number of data points during training, thus giving rise to unfairness where the learned model behaves differently across clients. To address these issues, we propose FAFL (i.e, $Q_a$-weighted loss in Definition 1) where different weights are assigned to different clients, and the learner must learn a model that is favorable for any weighted losses over an uncertainty set Q of possible weights. In this way, FAFL offers performance guarantees for any weighted client losses over $Q_\alpha$ which might include the true unknown target objective. Furthermore, we prove that FAFL (i.e, $Q_a$-weighted loss) is equivalent to a fairness measure HCVaR. Therefore, minimizing FAFL can also help improve fairness.

> How to set proper $a_i$?

Thanks. First, if we have some prior knowledge about which client’s data is the hardest one to distinguish from others, for example, in Fashion-MNIST, it is known that the shirt class is hardest one, we can choose small $a_i$ for that client to highlight its importance in achieving fairness. But in practice, that prior is usually unknown. Therefore, the hyperparameters $a_i$s need be tuned for different tasks. When the number of clients is small as in Fashion-MNIST dataset, we can search the best $a_i$s for each client on a grid (See Table 3) and then report the best performance. When the number of clients is large as in Vehicle and Sent140, we can choose the same $a$ for all (or most) clients and then only tune this common $a$, which greatly reduces the computational cost and also achieves good performance. See Table 4 in Appendix H.

> FAFL is defined as a framework, and HCVaR is defined as a risk value but the conclusion claims that these two terms are equivalent.

We apologize for confusion caused. FAFL is also referred to $Q_a$-weighted loss (see Definition 1) in the paper. Then, by lemma 1, $Q_a$-weighted loss is equivalent to HCVaR.

content.main_review:

Typos

content.title: Response to Reviewer r8PQ
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and would like to address the reviewer’s concerns as follows.

> The relationship between Def1 and Equation (29) of [Williamson and Menon, 2019].

Thanks. We first clarify that our Definition 1 is different from (29) of [Williamson and Menon, 2019] in the sense that we consider a worst-case weighted losses over an uncertainty set $Q_\alpha$ of possible weights whereas (29) is just a weighted loss with respect to a specific weighting. In fact, (29) is special case of Defintion 1 if choosing $Q_\alpha={v_S}$. Second, the problem we are solving is different. We use Def 1 as the true underlying FL objective function (i.e., the mixture weight) is unknown because of statistical heterogeneity. To address this issue, we propose to learn a model that is favorable for any weighted loss over an uncertainty set $Q_\alpha$. In contrast, Williamson and Menon (2019) apply a weighting to privilege certain groups. Finally, we prove that Definition 1 has a dual representation which connects to fairness. However, this formulation has not been discussed in theirs.

> See for instance ["Federated Composite Optimization", Yuan et al., ICML'21]. And please provide empirical evaluations of the simple subgradient-based methods.

Thanks. Yuan et al. (2021) also assume the smoothness condition. See Assumption 1(c). On Sent140 dataset, the average, worst 10$%$, Best $10%$ and variance of the test accuracy for subgradient-based methods are 69.9%, 26.7%, 100.0% and 505 respectively, which is worse than our proposed algorithm but still be better than other baselines. 

> Comparison to [Khaled et al. (2019)].

Thanks. Khaled et al. (2019) assumes a convex loss function and derives the convergence bound for local GD with heterogeneous data which is $O(1/T)+an\ error\ term$. This result is similar to our Theorem 1 (full participation case). However, we further consider the case of partial participation where only a subset of clients performs local updates. The partial participation case is more practical especially when the number of clients is large. We derive a convergence rate for that in Theorem 2 whereas partial participation is not considered in Khaled et al. (2019). We should mention that the analysis for partial participation is much more complicated as the randomly selected subset of clients varies each round. To overcome this difficulty, we introduce a virtual sequence and rewrite the update rule of algorithm 1.

> Is the value of q optimized for q-FFL? 

In the experimental section, we tune a best q for q-FFL following the same procedure as (Li et al., 2020a) and report its best performance.

> Why does $\hat{F}$ in (4) and (5) depend on w and $\eta$ and $(w*, \eta*) =argmin\ \hat{F}?$ Isn't $\hat{F}$ a constant?

We apologize for confusion caused. The expectation which we aim to minimize in (4) or (5) rather than the minimal is denoted as $\hat{F}$.
